claims.text: An augmented model incorporating realistic defect distributions and 1 wt.% oxygen effects will predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr transport properties more accurately than conventional perfect-crystal analytical models.
The relevant low-temperature regime is approximately 0–200 K.
The relevant high-temperature regime is approximately 300–1200 K.
The augmented model will parameterize point defects, grain boundaries, and scattering caused by 1 wt.% oxygen.
Pristine and 1 wt.% oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr specimens have measurements in both stated temperature regimes.
Lattice defects and oxygen atoms act as scattering centers in bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
The spatial distributions of defects and oxygen modify lattice dynamics and transport processes.
At low temperature, defect- and impurity-induced local lattice distortions enhance scattering.
Enhanced low-temperature scattering reduces conductivity relative to an ideal crystal.
At high temperature, anharmonic phonon scattering, defects, and oxygen-mediated mid-gap states modify transport.
Explicitly modeling the proposed scattering effects will improve predictive accuracy.
The augmented model will predict electrical or thermal conductivity within approximately 10–15% of experiment.
Conventional defect-free analytical approaches typically deviate from relevant experimental measurements by more than 20%.
Perfect-crystal analytical models exhibit significant discrepancies for materials containing realistic defect levels and oxygen impurities.
The proposed model applies to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with controlled defect levels and no more than 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed model's applicability outside 0–200 K and 300–1200 K, or above 1 wt.% oxygen, is unverified.
Prediction accuracy will depend on the actual defect distributions and oxygen placements.
Failure to reduce prediction error by at least approximately 10% relative to conventional models across both temperature regimes will falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to reproduce the experimentally observed transport difference caused by 1 wt.% oxygen will falsify the hypothesis.
